lessons.title: Anglo-Saxon Government, Economy & Society
lessons.description: How Anglo-Saxon England was governed, its economy worked, and the Church shaped daily life.
lessons.content_html:
The Power of the Anglo-Saxon Monarchy

By 1060, Anglo-Saxon England was one of the most advanced kingdoms in Europe. The king sat at the top of government and was expected to maintain law and order, defend the kingdom, and collect taxes. However, the king did not rule alone — he relied on a network of earls, a council of advisors called the Witan, and the Church to govern effectively.

Key Fact

The Witan was a council of around 30–60 leading nobles and churchmen who advised the king. They could influence major decisions and even had a role in choosing the next king when a monarch died.

The king’s authority was personal — he had to earn the loyalty of his earls through gifts of land and favour. If an earl grew too powerful, the balance of power could shift. This tension between royal authority and the power of the earls was a constant feature of Anglo-Saxon politics. Kings who lost the support of their leading nobles could face rebellion or even deposition, so maintaining good relationships was essential.

Earldoms and Local Government

England was divided into earldoms, each governed by an earl. By the 1060s, the four main earldoms were Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria, and East Anglia. Earls collected taxes, raised armies, and enforced the law in their region. In return, they kept a share of taxes and legal fines. Below the earls, thegns served as local lords, managing smaller estates and providing military service.

Justice was delivered through two main courts. Shire courts met twice a year to deal with serious crimes and land disputes, presided over by the earl or the king’s representative (the shire reeve). Hundred courts met every four weeks and handled more routine matters like theft and minor disputes. The system relied on community involvement — local people acted as witnesses and helped decide guilt through oaths and, in some cases, trial by ordeal (such as holding hot iron), where God was believed to reveal the truth.

The Economy and Social System

Anglo-Saxon England had a largely agricultural economy. Most people were ceorls (free peasants) who farmed strips of land in open fields around their village. Below them were villeins and slaves, who had fewer rights and freedoms. The social hierarchy ran from the king at the top, through earls and thegns, down to ceorls and slaves at the bottom. A person’s wergild (literally “man price”) reflected their position in this hierarchy — if someone was killed, the compensation owed to their family was determined by their social rank. An earl’s wergild was far higher than a ceorl’s, reflecting the value placed on status.

Key Fact

About 10% of England’s population were slaves in 1066. Slavery was an accepted part of Anglo-Saxon society, though the Church encouraged freeing slaves as an act of piety.

Towns like London, Winchester, and York were important centres of trade. England exported wool, metalwork, and embroidery, and imported wine, spices, and luxury goods from Europe. The coinage system was one of the most sophisticated in Europe — silver pennies were the standard currency, minted under royal authority at around 70 mints across the country. The king controlled the money supply by periodically recalling coins and issuing new ones, generating revenue in the process. This level of monetary control was unmatched in most of Europe and shows how advanced Anglo-Saxon government was.

Towns and Villages

Most Anglo-Saxons lived in small villages of 100–300 people. Farming followed the open-field system, where land was divided into strips and shared among villagers. Each village typically had two or three large fields that were farmed in rotation, with one left fallow each year to recover its fertility. Villages were largely self-sufficient, producing their own food, clothing, and tools. Towns were fewer and smaller than villages, but they served as centres for markets, crafts, and church administration. Major towns such as London had populations of around 10,000–15,000, making them significant urban centres by medieval European standards.

The Church was central to Anglo-Saxon life. It shaped education, morality, and law. Bishops and abbots sat on the Witan and advised the king. Monasteries were centres of learning, producing manuscripts and preserving knowledge. The Church owned around a quarter of all land in England and collected tithes (a tenth of each person’s produce) to fund its work. Parish churches were the heart of village life — everyone was expected to attend, and the Church marked every stage of life from baptism to burial.

Archbishops of Canterbury and York were the most powerful churchmen. By 1060, the Church in England had some practices that differed from those in Rome, such as married clergy and the buying and selling of Church positions (simony). These issues would become significant after the Norman Conquest.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “Describe two features” questions (4 marks), choose two distinct features and support each with a specific detail. For example, if asked to describe two features of Anglo-Saxon government, you could write about the role of earls (with the detail that they collected taxes and raised armies) and the Witan (with the detail that it advised the king and helped choose his successor). Avoid vague statements — the examiner wants precise knowledge.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Anglo-Saxon England was governed through a system of earls, thegns, and local courts, with the Witan advising the king on major decisions.
  • The economy was agricultural, based on the open-field system, with towns serving as centres of trade and craft. Silver pennies were the standard currency.
  • The Church was deeply embedded in government, education, and daily life, owning around a quarter of all land and collecting tithes from the population.

practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a developed explanation:
• One cause was that earls governed large regions (earldoms) on the king's behalf (1). They collected taxes, raised local armies, and enforced the law in their earldom (1). This gave them control over men and money in their region (1). As a result, a powerful earl like Harold Godwinson could become more influential than the king himself (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Anglo-Saxon system of government was effective before 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Target: AO1/AO2. Students may use stimulus points but must also use their own knowledge.
Top band (10-12): Explains reasons with a sustained, developed, and well-supported argument.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Explains reasons with some development.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Identifies and describes reasons.
Lower band (1-3): Simple or generalised statements.
Indicative content:
• The division of England into earldoms allowed effective local governance — earls enforced law, collected taxes, and raised armies.
• The Witan provided a system of counsel and consent, helping the king make legitimate decisions and choose successors.
• Shire and hundred courts provided regular access to justice at local level, involving communities through oaths and ordeals.
• The Church supported government through education, record-keeping, and moral authority, with bishops sitting on the Witan.
• The coinage system gave the king control over the money supply and facilitated trade.

practice_questions.text: 'The most important feature of Anglo-Saxon society was the power of the Church.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Target: AO1/AO2. Requires a judgement.
Top band (13-16): Complex explanation with a sustained, reasoned judgement. Both sides considered with a clear conclusion.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Developed explanation with a judgement, but may lack balance.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Simple explanation with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Basic statements with little or no explanation.
Indicative content:
AGREE:
• The Church owned ~25% of land and collected tithes, making it the wealthiest institution after the Crown.
• Bishops and abbots sat on the Witan, directly influencing royal policy.
• The Church controlled education, morality, and record-keeping — essential functions of government.
• Parish churches were central to daily life in every village.
DISAGREE:
• The king held supreme authority and could grant or remove earldoms.
• Earls wielded military and financial power in their regions — the Godwin family dominated English politics.
• The legal system (shire and hundred courts) operated largely through secular structures.
• Trade and the economy functioned independently of the Church.
Best answers will reach a supported judgement weighing relative importance.

lessons.title: The Succession Crisis & Rival Claimants
lessons.description: Why Edward the Confessor's death triggered a four-way fight for the English throne in 1066.
lessons.content_html:
The House of Godwin

By the 1060s, the house of Godwin was the most powerful family in England after the king. Earl Godwin had risen to control the earldom of Wessex — the wealthiest region — and married his daughter Edith to King Edward the Confessor. When Godwin died in 1053, his son Harold Godwinson inherited the earldom of Wessex and became the most influential figure in English politics.

Harold’s brothers also held earldoms: Tostig governed Northumbria, Gyrth held East Anglia, and Leofwine controlled the south-east. Together, the Godwins controlled most of England. This concentration of power made the family indispensable to Edward but also created resentment among other nobles.

Key Fact

By 1065, the Godwin family controlled four of England’s six earldoms. Harold Godwinson was effectively running the country, as Edward the Confessor grew old and increasingly focused on religion.

Harold’s Embassy to Normandy

In 1064, Harold travelled to Normandy. The exact reason remains disputed. Norman sources (especially the Bayeux Tapestry) claim Harold was sent by Edward to confirm William as his heir and that Harold swore an oath over holy relics to support William’s claim. English sources suggest Harold may have gone to rescue family hostages held by William. Whatever the truth, the Normans used this oath as powerful propaganda to justify William’s invasion. The oath was especially significant because swearing on holy relics was considered sacred and binding — breaking such an oath was not just a political betrayal but a sin against God, giving William moral authority as well as a political claim.

In 1065, the thegns of Northumbria revolted against Tostig Godwinson, Harold’s brother. They accused Tostig of ruling harshly, imposing heavy taxes, and murdering rivals. The rebels invited Morcar, brother of Earl Edwin of Mercia, to replace Tostig as Earl of Northumbria. Harold chose not to support his brother, instead negotiating a peaceful solution that accepted Morcar as the new earl. Tostig was exiled and went abroad, nursing a bitter grudge against Harold. This decision weakened Harold’s family power but secured the loyalty of the powerful Mercian earls Edwin and Morcar — at least temporarily.

The Death of Edward the Confessor

Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066 without a clear heir. On his deathbed, Edward reportedly reached out to Harold and commended the kingdom to his protection. This deathbed nomination gave Harold a powerful claim, and the Witan quickly confirmed him as king the very next day. Harold was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 6 January — the speed of his coronation was deliberate, designed to present other claimants with a fait accompli. However, Edward’s failure to produce children and his contradictory promises about the succession created a crisis that would be settled by war.

The Rival Claimants

Four men had a claim to the English throne in January 1066, each based on different grounds:

Key Fact

The four claimants were Harold Godwinson (deathbed nomination + Witan approval), William of Normandy (claimed Edward promised him the throne + Harold’s oath), Harald Hardrada (based on an agreement between earlier kings of Norway and England), and Edgar the Aethling (Edward’s great-nephew and the closest blood relative).

Harold Godwinson: Strongest position — the Witan chose him, he had Edward’s deathbed blessing, he was the most powerful earl, and he was English. His weakness was that he had no royal blood and had arguably broken an oath to William.

William of Normandy: Claimed Edward promised him the throne during a visit in 1051 and that Harold swore to support this. He also secured papal backing from Pope Alexander II. His weakness was that he was a foreigner with no support inside England.

Harald Hardrada: King of Norway, an experienced warrior. His claim rested on an agreement between King Magnus of Norway and Harthacnut that if either died without an heir, the other would inherit both kingdoms. This was a weak legal claim but backed by military force.

Edgar the Aethling: The closest blood relative to Edward — his great-nephew. However, he was only about 14 years old in 1066, had no political experience, no military following, and no powerful supporters.

The succession crisis of 1066 arose because Anglo-Saxon kingship was not simply hereditary. The Witan had the right to choose the most suitable candidate, and “suitability” meant military ability and political support as much as bloodline. This opened the door to multiple competing claims. In continental Europe, where hereditary succession was more established, Edgar the Aethling’s blood claim would have been decisive. But in England, the Witan’s power to choose a “capable” king over a young, inexperienced heir made the succession a political contest rather than a legal certainty. This fundamental difference helps explain why four men believed they had a legitimate right to the English throne.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “Explain why” questions (12 marks) on the succession crisis, structure your answer around multiple reasons and show how they connect. For example, explain why there was a crisis (Edward had no children, he made contradictory promises, Anglo-Saxon succession was not purely hereditary) and develop each reason with specific evidence. The best answers link causes together — for instance, Edward’s childlessness only became a crisis because he had apparently promised the throne to more than one person.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Godwin family dominated Anglo-Saxon politics, controlling most earldoms by 1065 — but Tostig’s exile in 1065 weakened the family and created an enemy who would ally with Hardrada.
  • Edward the Confessor died in January 1066 without a clear heir, triggering a succession crisis with four rival claimants — Harold, William, Hardrada, and Edgar.
  • Each claimant based their case on different grounds (nomination, promise, treaty, blood) — the crisis existed because Anglo-Saxon kingship was not purely hereditary.

• The power of the Godwin family meant Harold was in the strongest position — but William had papal backing and military resources.

lessons.title: Stamford Bridge & the Battle of Hastings
lessons.description: How Harold defeated Hardrada at Stamford Bridge but lost to William at Hastings weeks later.
lessons.content_html:
Harold’s Coronation and Early Reign

Harold Godwinson was crowned king on 6 January 1066 — the day after Edward the Confessor’s death. The speed of the coronation was deliberate: Harold needed to establish his authority before rivals could challenge him. The Witan had approved Harold’s claim, and Archbishop Stigand performed the ceremony at Westminster Abbey.

Harold spent the spring and summer of 1066 preparing for invasion. He positioned his fyrd (part-time peasant army) along the south coast to watch for William’s fleet, while his fleet patrolled the English Channel. By September, supplies were running low and the fyrd’s service period had expired, so Harold was forced to disband them — just as the threats materialised.

The Battle of Gate Fulford — 20 September 1066

While Harold watched the south, Harald Hardrada and Tostig landed in northern England with around 300 ships and 8,000–10,000 warriors. Earls Edwin and Morcar marched to meet them at Gate Fulford, near York, on 20 September. The English earls were decisively defeated. This victory gave Hardrada control of York and forced him to wait at Stamford Bridge for hostages and supplies.

Key Fact

The Battle of Gate Fulford (20 September 1066) was a significant Norman-era battle because the defeat of Edwin and Morcar’s forces meant the northern English army was destroyed. Harold had to march north with his own troops to deal with Hardrada, leaving the south coast undefended.

The Battle of Stamford Bridge — 25 September 1066

Harold reacted with remarkable speed. He marched his housecarls nearly 190 miles from London to Yorkshire in just four days, gathering local forces as he went. On 25 September, he caught Hardrada’s army completely by surprise at Stamford Bridge. The Norwegians were relaxing without their armour on a warm day, expecting no resistance.

The battle was fierce and decisive. Both Harald Hardrada and Tostig were killed. The Norwegian army was shattered — of the roughly 300 ships that arrived, only around 24 were needed to carry the survivors home. It was a stunning victory for Harold. However, the battle cost Harold many experienced fighters, and his army was exhausted from the forced march.

Just two days after Stamford Bridge, on 27 September, the wind changed and William’s fleet set sail from Normandy. William landed at Pevensey on 28 September with around 7,000 troops, including cavalry, archers, and infantry. Harold received the news and immediately turned his exhausted army around, marching roughly 250 miles south in about 10 days. He arrived near Hastings on 13 October, choosing to fight the next morning on a ridge at Senlac Hill.

The Battle of Hastings — 14 October 1066

Harold positioned his army on the high ground of Senlac Hill, forming a tight shield wall. His force of around 7,000–8,000 troops was mostly infantry: housecarls with axes and swords at the front, and fyrd men behind. Harold had no archers and no cavalry to speak of.

Morning

Norman attacks repelled

William sent his archers, then infantry, then cavalry up the hill. The shield wall held firm. Norman infantry struggled against the steep slope and the devastating two-handed axes of the housecarls.

Midday

Rumour of William’s death

A rumour spread that William had been killed. He lifted his helmet to show his face and rallied his troops. The Bretons on the left flank broke and fled, and some English fyrd broke ranks to chase them down the hill.

Afternoon

Feigned retreats

William used feigned retreats to lure English troops out of their strong defensive position. Each time the English broke ranks to pursue, Norman cavalry turned and cut them down.

Evening

Harold’s death

As the shield wall thinned, a final combined assault of archers (firing high) and cavalry broke through. Harold was killed — tradition says by an arrow to the eye, though this is debated. The English army fled.

Key Fact

William won the Battle of Hastings because of a combination of factors: his use of combined arms (archers, infantry, cavalry), the effectiveness of feigned retreats, Harold’s tired and depleted army, the lack of English cavalry and archers, and Harold’s death on the battlefield which destroyed English morale.

William’s leadership: He was a skilled commander who adapted his tactics during the battle, using feigned retreats and rallying his troops when they thought he was dead. Norman troops and tactics: William used a combined force of archers, infantry, and cavalry, giving him flexibility that Harold lacked. Harold’s weaknesses: Harold’s army was exhausted from Stamford Bridge and the forced marches. He had no archers or cavalry. Some of his best housecarls had been killed or wounded in the north. Luck and timing: The wind changed at the worst possible moment for Harold. If William had sailed earlier, Harold would have had his full fyrd waiting. Harold’s death ended the battle — without their king, the English had no reason to fight on.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “Explain why” (12 marks) on William’s victory at Hastings, use the stimulus points but always add your own knowledge. A common mistake is only describing what happened. Instead, explain why each factor mattered. For example, don’t just say “Harold marched south quickly” — explain that this meant his army was tired and depleted, which reduced his ability to hold the shield wall throughout the day.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Harold won a stunning victory at Stamford Bridge (25 September 1066), destroying Hardrada’s army — but it left his forces exhausted and depleted before facing William.
  • William won at Hastings (14 October 1066) through combined arms, feigned retreats, Harold’s tiredness, and Harold’s death — no single factor explains the outcome.
  • The Battle of Hastings changed English history forever — it ended Anglo-Saxon rule and began the Norman Conquest.

lessons.title: William Establishing Control: Castles & Rewards
lessons.description: How William secured power after Hastings through submission of earls, castles, and loyal followers.
lessons.content_html:
The Submission of the Earls, 1066

After his victory at Hastings, William did not march straight to London. Instead, he moved through southern England, burning and raiding to intimidate potential opponents. He seized Dover and Canterbury before circling around London. The remaining English leaders — including Edgar the Aethling, Archbishop Stigand, and Earls Edwin and Morcar — initially considered resistance. However, faced with William’s military strength and the lack of any united English force, they submitted to William at Berkhamsted in December 1066.

William was crowned King of England on Christmas Day 1066 at Westminster Abbey. The coronation ceremony followed Anglo-Saxon traditions to give his rule an air of legitimacy. However, when the congregation shouted their approval, Norman soldiers outside mistook the noise for a riot and began setting fire to nearby buildings. This was a sign of the tension and mistrust that would define the early years of Norman rule.

Key Fact

The English leaders submitted at Berkhamsted because they had no army capable of stopping William. Edgar the Aethling was too young and inexperienced to lead resistance. The submission gave William a veneer of legitimacy — the English appeared to accept him voluntarily.

Rewarding Followers

William rewarded his loyal Norman followers with English land and titles. This achieved two things: it secured the loyalty of his followers by giving them a stake in England, and it replaced the Anglo-Saxon elite with Normans who owed everything to William. Key supporters like William fitzOsbern and Odo of Bayeux (William’s half-brother) received vast estates. FitzOsbern became Earl of Hereford, and Odo became Earl of Kent.

Initially, William tried to work alongside some Anglo-Saxon earls. Edwin and Morcar were allowed to keep their earldoms, and some English thegns retained their lands. This policy of limited cooperation was pragmatic — William did not have enough Normans to replace every English landowner. He simply could not govern a country of around 2 million people with the few thousand Normans who had crossed the Channel. However, as rebellions broke out from 1068 onwards, William increasingly replaced English lords with Normans. Each rebellion provided a pretext for confiscation: rebels forfeited their lands, which were then redistributed to loyal Norman followers. By the time of the Domesday Book in 1086, the transfer was nearly complete.

The Marcher Earldoms

William created powerful Marcher earldoms on England’s vulnerable borders. These were placed at Chester (to guard against the Welsh in the north-west), Shrewsbury (to defend the Welsh border), and Hereford (to protect the south-west border). The Marcher earls had greater powers than ordinary earls — they could raise armies, build castles, and administer justice without direct royal permission. This was necessary because the borders were far from London and needed rapid military responses.

The Marcher earldoms solved a practical problem: England’s borders with Wales and Scotland were constantly threatened, but William could not be everywhere at once. By giving trusted followers extra powers in these regions, William ensured rapid military responses to border threats without needing to intervene personally. However, this created a risk — overly powerful Marcher earls could potentially challenge the king, as the revolt of 1075 would later show.

Castle Building

Castle building was central to Norman control. The Normans introduced motte-and-bailey castles to England on a massive scale. These could be built quickly — some in as little as two weeks — using forced Anglo-Saxon labour. By 1086, William had ordered the construction of around 500 castles across England.

Key Fact

Motte-and-bailey castles served three purposes: military (a garrison could control the surrounding area and respond quickly to rebellion), psychological (the imposing structure reminded the local population of Norman power), and administrative (the castle became the centre of local government, replacing Anglo-Saxon meeting places).

The motte was a large mound of earth, sometimes 5–10 metres high, with a wooden tower (or later a stone keep) on top. It was the last point of defence. The bailey was an enclosed courtyard at the base of the motte, surrounded by a wooden palisade (fence) and a ditch. It contained stables, workshops, storage buildings, and accommodation for soldiers. A drawbridge or steps connected the bailey to the motte. Key early castles included the Tower of London, Warwick Castle, and castles at York, Lincoln, and Exeter.

William strategically placed castles at key locations: river crossings, road junctions, and in major towns. This allowed small Norman garrisons of perhaps 20–50 soldiers to control populations of thousands. The castle at York, for example, dominated the main route into northern England. The building of castles often required demolishing Anglo-Saxon homes — in Lincoln, 166 houses were destroyed to make room for the castle. This destruction deepened resentment among the English population and became a source of future rebellion, but it also demonstrated beyond any doubt who was now in charge.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on how William established control, always link methods together. Castles, rewards, and the Marcher earldoms were not separate strategies — they worked as a system. For “Explain why” questions, show how each method reinforced the others. For example, castles were built by the followers William rewarded with land, and Marcher earls used castles to defend the borders.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • William secured power through a combination of military intimidation (burning and raiding), political calculation (coronation at Westminster, allowing some English earls to keep their positions), and rewarding followers with land and titles.
  • Marcher earldoms at Chester, Shrewsbury, and Hereford gave trusted earls extra powers to defend England’s borders against Welsh and Scottish threats.
  • Motte-and-bailey castles were the backbone of Norman control — quick to build, they served as military bases, symbols of power, and centres of local administration.

Best answers will argue that these methods worked as a system — castles without loyal garrisons would be useless, and loyal followers without castles would struggle to control hostile territory.

lessons.title: Anglo-Saxon Resistance & the Harrying of the North
lessons.description: Why Anglo-Saxons rebelled against William and how the Harrying of the North crushed resistance.
lessons.content_html:
The Revolt of Edwin & Morcar, 1068

Although Earls Edwin and Morcar had submitted to William at Berkhamsted, they grew increasingly resentful of Norman rule. William had promised Edwin a marriage to one of his daughters, but the marriage never happened. Norman lords were being given English lands, and Edwin and Morcar felt their power slipping away.

In 1068, Edwin and Morcar fled north and raised a rebellion. William responded with his usual speed and force. He marched north, building castles at Warwick and Nottingham on the way to demonstrate his power. The rebellion collapsed without a major battle — Edwin and Morcar submitted again, and William built a castle at York to tighten his grip on the north. He also placed a Norman, Robert de Comines, as the new Earl of Northumbria to assert direct control over the region. However, the underlying causes of resentment remained: heavy taxation, loss of land, and the replacement of English lords with Normans. The north would soon revolt again, with far more devastating consequences.

Edgar the Aethling and the Northern Rebellions, 1069

In January 1069, the Norman-appointed Earl of Northumbria, Robert de Comines, was killed along with 900 of his men when the people of Durham rose in revolt. This triggered a wider northern rebellion. Edgar the Aethling returned from exile in Scotland and joined the rebels. The northern English attacked and destroyed William’s castle at York, killing the Norman garrison.

Key Fact

In the summer of 1069, a Danish fleet of around 240 ships arrived in the Humber, sent by King Sweyn of Denmark. The Danes allied with Edgar and the northern rebels, creating the most serious threat William had faced since Hastings. Together they captured York.

William marched north once more. He bribed the Danish fleet to withdraw (they would leave in spring 1070) and then systematically destroyed the rebellion. But this time, William did not simply rebuild his castles and accept submissions. He decided to make an example of the north that would prevent rebellion from ever happening again.

Hereward the Wake was an Anglo-Saxon thegn who led the last major English resistance. In 1070, he allied with a Danish raiding force and attacked the wealthy monastery at Peterborough. When the Danes withdrew, Hereward retreated to the Isle of Ely in the marshy Fens of East Anglia — a natural fortress surrounded by impassable wetlands.

Earl Morcar and other rebels joined Hereward at Ely. William besieged the island, building a causeway across the marshes. When the causeway reportedly collapsed, he tried other approaches. Eventually, the monks of Ely showed the Normans a secret path through the marshes (possibly bribed or threatened). The rebellion collapsed in 1071. Morcar was captured and imprisoned for life. Hereward’s fate is uncertain — some sources say he escaped and was later pardoned, while others say he was killed. The fall of Ely marked the end of organised Anglo-Saxon resistance.

The Harrying of the North, 1069–70

The Harrying of the North was William’s most brutal act. Over the winter of 1069–70, William’s army systematically destroyed everything between the Humber and the Tees — and later extended the destruction to Cheshire and Shropshire. Crops were burned, livestock slaughtered, farming tools and seed corn destroyed, villages razed, and wells poisoned. The aim was total devastation: to make the region incapable of supporting rebellion.

Key Fact

The chronicler Orderic Vitalis wrote that over 100,000 people died of famine following the Harrying. While this figure may be exaggerated, the Domesday Book (1086) recorded vast areas of northern England as “waste” — land that was still unproductive 17 years later. Some historians consider it an act of genocide.

Immediate impact: Mass famine across the north of England. Refugees fled south or to Scotland. Communities that had existed for centuries were wiped out. Land values collapsed — the north became the poorest region of England.

Long-term impact: The north never again posed a serious military threat to William. The Domesday Book (1086) still recorded huge areas as “waste” — showing the north had not recovered even after 17 years. The Harrying demonstrated that William would use extreme violence to maintain control, deterring future rebellion elsewhere. It also generated lasting bitterness and is considered by some historians as the darkest chapter of the Norman Conquest.

The Harrying achieved its military objective: the north was broken as a source of resistance. There were no further northern rebellions during William’s reign. But the human cost was enormous. Refugees fled south or crossed into Scotland, and some sources describe survivors resorting to cannibalism. The Harrying shaped the character of Norman rule for decades to come — demonstrating that William’s power ultimately rested on the threat of extreme violence. Even the normally sympathetic chronicler Orderic Vitalis, himself half-Norman, wrote that William would have to answer to God for the suffering he caused.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on the Harrying of the North, always distinguish between immediate and long-term impact. Immediate: famine, refugees, destroyed communities. Long-term: the north never rebelled again, Domesday “waste” entries 17 years later. For “How far do you agree?” questions, consider both effectiveness (it worked) and consequences (human cost, resentment). The best answers show that the Harrying can be judged differently depending on the criteria used.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Anglo-Saxon resistance included the revolt of Edwin & Morcar (1068), Edgar and the northern rebellions with Danish support (1069), and Hereward the Wake at Ely (1070–71) — each was defeated by William’s speed and military strength.
  • The Harrying of the North (1069–70) was William’s most brutal response — systematic destruction of crops, livestock, and villages caused mass famine and ensured the north could never rebel again.
  • The Domesday Book (1086) still recorded large areas as “waste” 17 years later, showing the long-term devastation of the Harrying.

lessons.title: The Feudal System & Norman Government
lessons.description: How the feudal system and centralised Norman government replaced Anglo-Saxon structures after 1066.
lessons.content_html:
The Feudal Hierarchy

After the Conquest, William imposed the feudal system on England. The core principle was simple: all land belonged to the king. William granted large estates to his most loyal followers, known as tenants-in-chief (about 200 men, including bishops and abbots). In return, they owed the king military service, loyalty, and financial contributions.

Tenants-in-chief then granted portions of their land to knights, who received enough land to support themselves and their families in return for fighting when called upon. A knight’s estate was known as a “knight’s fee” — the amount of land needed to equip and maintain one mounted warrior. Below the knights were peasants who worked the land, paying rent and providing labour service (typically two or three days per week on their lord’s fields). This created a clear chain of obligation running from the bottom to the top, with each level owing service to the one above.

Key Fact

The feudal system worked through homage (a public ceremony where a lord knelt and swore loyalty to his superior), knight service (providing a set number of armed knights, usually for 40 days per year), and forfeiture (land could be taken back if a lord broke his oath or rebelled). This gave William control over every level of society.

Landholding and the Nature of Feudalism

The feudal system transformed who held land in England. By 1086, the Domesday Book showed that only two major English landholders remained out of approximately 200 tenants-in-chief. Almost all land had been transferred from Anglo-Saxon to Norman hands. This was the most complete change of landownership in English history.

Homage: A formal ceremony where a vassal (lord or knight) knelt before his superior, placed his hands between his lord’s hands, and swore an oath of loyalty. This created a binding public agreement. Knight service: The obligation to provide armed and trained knights for military campaigns, typically 40 days per year. Tenants-in-chief had to supply specific quotas based on the size of their estates. Labour service: Peasants owed their lord a set number of days’ work on his fields each week, in addition to working their own strips. Forfeiture: If a lord broke his oath of loyalty or rebelled, the king could seize all his lands and redistribute them. This was William’s ultimate sanction and a powerful deterrent against disloyalty.

Changes to Government: Centralised Power

Norman government was more centralised than Anglo-Saxon government. William dramatically reduced the number of earls. Instead of the four great Anglo-Saxon earldoms (Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria, East Anglia), William kept power concentrated in his own hands and those of a small circle of trusted followers. He limited earls’ independence to prevent any single nobleman from becoming powerful enough to challenge him — having seen how the Godwin family had dominated Edward the Confessor.

When William was absent from England (he spent roughly half his reign in Normandy), he appointed regents to govern in his place. His most common regents were Odo of Bayeux and Archbishop Lanfranc. This system worked because William chose men who were loyal and capable, but it also created risks — a regent who abused power could cause resentment and rebellion, as Odo later proved.

Key Fact

William reduced the power of earls compared to Anglo-Saxon times. Anglo-Saxon earls like the Godwins had controlled entire regions with their own armies and revenues. Norman earls held land scattered across multiple counties, preventing them from building a local power base strong enough to challenge the king.

The Sheriff and the Royal Demesne

The sheriff became the most important local royal official under the Normans. Sheriffs administered each shire on the king’s behalf, collected taxes, presided over shire courts, and managed the royal demesne (the king’s own estates). William increasingly appointed Norman sheriffs to replace Anglo-Saxon ones, ensuring his agents controlled local government. The sheriff was effectively the king’s eyes and ears in each shire — he reported directly to the king and could override local lords if necessary. The royal demesne itself was extensive, providing William with direct income independent of his tenants-in-chief.

William introduced the concept of the royal forest — vast areas of land reserved for the king’s hunting. The New Forest in Hampshire was the most famous, created by William around 1079. Forest law was separate from ordinary law and extremely harsh: killing a deer could be punished by blinding or mutilation. Forests were not just woodland — they included farmland, villages, and open heath, all subject to the king’s exclusive hunting rights.

By the time of the Domesday Book, royal forests covered perhaps a third of England. Forest law was deeply unpopular because it restricted grazing, woodcutting, and farming rights that Anglo-Saxons had previously enjoyed. It was a visible symbol of Norman oppression and royal power imposed on the landscape itself.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing Anglo-Saxon and Norman government, focus on change and continuity. Some structures continued (shire courts, sheriffs), but the nature of power changed dramatically (centralised royal control replaced powerful independent earls). For “How far do you agree?” questions, this allows you to argue both sides effectively.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The feudal system was based on land for loyalty: the king granted land to tenants-in-chief, who provided knights; obligations were enforced through homage, knight service, and forfeiture.
  • Norman government was more centralised than Anglo-Saxon — William limited earls’ power, used regents during absences, and appointed loyal Norman sheriffs to control local government.
  • Forest law and the royal demesne extended the king’s control over land and resources, while the Domesday Book showed near-total transfer of landownership from English to Norman hands by 1086.

lessons.title: The Norman Church, Lanfranc & the Domesday Book
lessons.description: How Lanfranc reformed the English Church and why the Domesday Book transformed Norman government.
lessons.content_html:
The Church’s Role in Norman England

The Church was essential to William’s rule. It provided educated administrators, moral authority, and a network of parish churches that reached every community in England. Bishops and abbots held land as tenants-in-chief under the feudal system, meaning they owed the king military service just like secular lords. The Church legitimised William’s rule — Pope Alexander II had blessed the invasion and sent a papal banner.

However, the Anglo-Saxon Church had problems by Norman standards. Some practices differed from continental norms, and the most prominent example of this was Archbishop Stigand.

The Significance of Stigand

Stigand had been Archbishop of Canterbury since 1052, but his position was controversial. He held two bishoprics at once (Canterbury and Winchester), which was against Church rules (pluralism). He had received his pallium (the symbol of papal authority) from an antipope — a pope later declared illegitimate. The papacy considered Stigand’s appointment invalid.

Key Fact

Stigand’s irregular position was one reason Pope Alexander II supported William’s invasion. William used papal backing to present the Conquest as a religious mission to reform the corrupt English Church. Stigand was finally deposed in 1070 and replaced by the Norman Lanfranc.

Lanfranc’s Reforms

Lanfranc was an Italian-born scholar and monk who had been abbot of William’s monastery at Caen in Normandy. As Archbishop of Canterbury from 1070, he carried out sweeping reforms of the English Church:

Replacing English churchmen: By 1087, only one English bishop (Wulfstan of Worcester) remained. All other bishops and most abbots were Norman. This was Normanisation of the Church in practice.

Ending corruption: Lanfranc attacked simony (buying and selling Church positions) and pluralism (holding multiple positions). He insisted on clerical celibacy (priests should not marry), though enforcement was patchy.

Reorganisation: Lanfranc established a clear hierarchy with Canterbury as the supreme archbishopric above York. He moved some bishoprics from rural villages to towns (e.g. from Dorchester to Lincoln) and introduced regular Church councils to standardise practice. He also rebuilt Canterbury Cathedral and many other churches in the grander Romanesque style.

Church courts: Lanfranc separated Church courts from secular courts. Previously, bishops had sat in shire courts alongside the sheriff. Now, Church courts handled moral and religious offences (like adultery and oath-breaking) separately from royal courts. This gave the Church greater independence in its own sphere but also extended its authority.

Lanfranc was also a loyal political ally of William. He served as regent when William was in Normandy and helped suppress the revolt of the earls in 1075, coordinating the military response that crushed the rebellion before William even returned. He was both a churchman and a political operator — his loyalty to William was crucial to the stability of Norman England. The partnership between William and Lanfranc illustrates how the Normans used the Church as a tool of government: bishops held land as tenants-in-chief, owed military service, and served in administrative roles alongside their religious duties.

The Domesday Survey and Domesday Book

In 1085, William ordered a comprehensive survey of all land and resources in England. The immediate trigger may have been the threat of a Danish invasion — William needed to know exactly what resources he could call upon. Commissioners were sent to every shire to record who owned each piece of land, what it was worth, how many people lived there, and what livestock and equipment they had. To ensure accuracy, a second set of commissioners checked the first group’s findings. The survey covered almost all of England (though some northern areas and major cities like London were omitted). The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle recorded that “not even one ox, one cow, or one pig escaped notice” — reflecting both the thoroughness of the survey and the resentment it caused.

Key Fact

The resulting Domesday Book (completed 1086) recorded three snapshots: who held the land in 1066 (under Edward the Confessor), who held it when William granted it, and who held it in 1086. This allowed William to settle disputes, prevent fraud, and see exactly how much the Conquest had changed England’s landownership.

For government: The Domesday Book gave William detailed knowledge of his kingdom’s resources. No medieval ruler had ever possessed such comprehensive information. It confirmed feudal landholding — once recorded in Domesday, ownership was legally fixed. It settled disputes over who owned what and prevented lords from claiming more than they were entitled to.

For finance: The survey revealed exactly what each estate was worth, allowing William to set fair (and maximum) tax levels. It prevented lords from hiding wealth or underreporting their resources. It confirmed that William could extract more revenue from England than any Anglo-Saxon king had managed.

For historians: The Domesday Book is the most detailed record of any medieval society in Europe. It reveals the extent of the Norman land transfer (almost total), the impact of the Harrying of the North (“waste” entries), and the structure of English society twenty years after the Conquest.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on Lanfranc and the Domesday Book often appear together because both relate to how William consolidated control. For “Explain why” questions, remember that Church reform and the Domesday survey were not just about religion or administration — they were tools of political control. Lanfranc replaced English churchmen with loyal Normans; the Domesday Book gave William unmatched knowledge of his kingdom’s wealth.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lanfranc reformed the English Church by replacing English bishops with Normans, attacking simony and pluralism, separating Church and secular courts, and asserting Canterbury’s supremacy over York.
  • Stigand’s irregular position gave William a justification for replacing the English Church leadership — Church reform served both religious and political purposes.
  • The Domesday Book (1086) gave William unprecedented knowledge of England’s land, wealth, and people — it was a tool of taxation, political control, and the definitive record of the Norman Conquest’s impact.

• A permanent administrative tool — the Domesday Book continued to be used for centuries.

lessons.title: The Revolt of the Earls & William’s Legacy
lessons.description: Why the 1075 revolt failed, Odo's fall from grace, and the disputed succession after William's death.
lessons.content_html:
The Revolt of the Earls, 1075

The revolt of 1075 was the last major rebellion against William’s rule in England. It was led by three earls: Roger de Breteuil (Earl of Hereford), Ralph de Gael (Earl of Norfolk), and Waltheof (Earl of Northumbria, the last surviving Anglo-Saxon earl).

The revolt was triggered by personal grievances. Roger was angry that William had refused permission for his marriage to Ralph’s sister. Both resented William’s increasing control over their affairs. The conspiracy was hatched at Ralph’s wedding feast. Waltheof’s involvement is unclear — he may have joined reluctantly and later confessed to Lanfranc.

Key Fact

William was in Normandy when the revolt broke out. The rebellion was crushed by his loyal regents and earls without William needing to return. Lanfranc coordinated the response, Bishop Wulfstan and the Abbot of Evesham blocked Roger in the west, and Odo of Bayeux defeated Ralph in the east. The rebellion collapsed before the rebels could join forces.

The revolt failed quickly. Roger was prevented from crossing the River Severn and was captured. Ralph fled to Brittany before the fighting ended. A Danish fleet arrived too late to help and raided York before withdrawing. Waltheof was the most controversial case — he had confessed to Lanfranc, possibly hoping for mercy. Instead, he was tried, found guilty, and beheaded in 1076. He was the only Englishman executed by William, and his death was widely seen as unjust by the English population.

The effects of the revolt were significant. Roger’s lands were forfeited and he was imprisoned for life. Ralph’s estates were confiscated. The earldom of Hereford and the earldom of Norfolk were effectively abolished. William never again allowed earls to hold the same level of power. The revolt proved that William’s system of castles, loyal followers, and regents could maintain control even in his absence.

Bishop Odo’s Career

Odo of Bayeux was William’s half-brother and one of the most powerful men in England. He was both Bishop of Bayeux and Earl of Kent, combining Church authority with secular power. He may have commissioned the Bayeux Tapestry to celebrate the Conquest. He served as regent during William’s absences and played a key role in crushing the 1075 revolt.

However, Odo became increasingly ambitious and corrupt. He accumulated vast wealth, built up a private army, and was accused of oppressing the people of Kent. In 1082, William arrested Odo and imprisoned him. The precise reasons remain debated — one theory is that Odo was planning to lead an army to Rome to make himself pope. William emphasised that he arrested Odo as Earl of Kent (a secular title), not as Bishop of Bayeux (a Church position), to avoid conflict with the papacy.

William’s Character and Legacy

William I was a complex figure. He was ruthless (the Harrying of the North, executing Waltheof), politically shrewd (using the Church, the feudal system, and the Domesday Book to control England), and militarily brilliant (winning Hastings, crushing every rebellion). He was deeply religious — he founded monasteries and supported Church reform. But he was also driven by an insatiable desire for control, as the Domesday survey and forest law demonstrated.

Key Fact

William died on 9 September 1087 after being injured when his horse stumbled on burning embers at the siege of Mantes in France. His death triggered another succession crisis, as he left his lands divided between his sons.

Relations with Robert and Robert’s Revolt

Robert Curthose was William’s eldest son. Their relationship was difficult. Robert was impatient for power and resented being given responsibility without real authority. In 1077–80, Robert openly revolted against his father. He allied with the King of France and even wounded William in battle (though he did not recognise his father at the time and was reportedly horrified when he realised). The revolt ended in an uneasy reconciliation, but the relationship remained strained.

On his deathbed, William divided his lands: Robert received Normandy (the ancestral homeland), and William Rufus (William’s second surviving son) received England. His youngest son, Henry, received money but no land. Odo was released from prison.

This division was a recipe for conflict. William Rufus raced to England and was crowned William II (William Rufus) on 26 September 1087. Many Norman lords held land on both sides of the Channel and had to choose between the two brothers. Odo, released from prison, immediately sided with Robert and led a revolt against William Rufus in 1088. The revolt failed — William Rufus secured the loyalty of the English people and key Norman barons by promising good government and lower taxes. Odo was defeated, lost his English lands, and was exiled to Normandy permanently.

William the Conqueror transformed England more profoundly than any ruler before or since. In just 21 years, he replaced the Anglo-Saxon ruling class, imposed the feudal system, built hundreds of castles, reformed the Church, and compiled the Domesday Book. Whether his legacy is viewed as the creation of a stronger, more centralised kingdom or as a brutal foreign conquest that destroyed Anglo-Saxon culture depends on perspective — and that debate is exactly what the exam is testing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on the revolt of 1075 or William’s legacy, think about significance. The 1075 revolt is significant not because it nearly succeeded (it didn’t) but because its rapid defeat proved the effectiveness of William’s control system. Similarly, the disputed succession after William’s death echoes the 1066 crisis — drawing this parallel can earn you marks for analysis and showing understanding of patterns across the period.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The revolt of 1075 was crushed by William’s regents without him returning from Normandy — proving that his system of castles, loyal followers, and regents could maintain control in his absence.
  • Odo of Bayeux rose to be one of the most powerful men in England but was imprisoned in 1082 for overreaching; he later sided with Robert against William Rufus in 1088 and was exiled.
  • William’s death in 1087 triggered a disputed succession: Robert received Normandy, William Rufus received England — the division caused conflict that echoed the crisis of 1066.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the revolt of the earls in 1075.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification + 1 for supporting detail):
• Feature 1: The revolt was led by Roger de Breteuil, Ralph de Gael, and Waltheof (1) — it was triggered by personal grievances, including William refusing Roger permission to marry (1).
• Feature 2: The revolt was crushed without William returning from Normandy (1) — Lanfranc coordinated the response, and loyal earls and bishops blocked the rebels before they could join forces (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the revolt of the earls in 1075.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a developed explanation:
• One consequence was that William further reduced the power of earls (1). Roger's and Ralph's earldoms were abolished and their lands confiscated (1). William never again allowed earls to hold the same level of power or independence (1). As a result, the revolt strengthened William's centralised control and proved that his system of governance could function without him being present (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Robert Curthose's revolt against William in 1077-80.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a developed explanation:
• One cause was Robert's frustration at being denied real power (1). As William's eldest son, Robert expected authority and independence, especially in Normandy (1). William gave Robert responsibility but no real decision-making power, treating him as subordinate (1). As a result, Robert allied with the King of France and took up arms against his father (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the revolt of the earls in 1075 failed. You may use the following in your answer: castles, Lanfranc. You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Target: AO1/AO2.
Top band (10-12): Explains reasons with a sustained, developed argument.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Explains reasons with some development.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Identifies and describes reasons.
Lower band (1-3): Simple or generalised statements.
Indicative content:
• Castles — William's network of castles meant loyal Norman garrisons controlled key routes and towns, preventing rebels from moving freely or joining forces.
• Lanfranc — as regent, Lanfranc coordinated the response efficiently, deploying loyal earls and bishops to block each rebel force separately.
• The rebels could not unite — Roger was blocked at the River Severn and Ralph was defeated in the east before they could combine their forces.
• Danish fleet arrived too late — by the time Scandinavian ships reached England, the revolt was already over.
• Waltheof may have betrayed the conspiracy by confessing to Lanfranc.
• William's feudal system meant most Norman lords were loyal — they had land to lose if William fell.

practice_questions.text: 'William I's greatest achievement was the feudal system.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Target: AO1/AO2. Requires a judgement.
Top band (13-16): Complex explanation with a sustained, reasoned judgement.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Developed explanation with a judgement.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Simple explanation with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Basic statements.
Indicative content:
AGREE:
• The feudal system gave William a reliable army through knight service and a loyal governing class through land grants.
• Forfeiture deterred rebellion — lords who revolted lost everything.
• Scattering estates prevented lords building regional power bases.
• The system lasted for centuries, shaping English society long after William's death.
DISAGREE:
• Castle building provided the physical infrastructure of control — ~500 castles by 1086.
• The Domesday Book gave William unprecedented administrative knowledge.
• Church reform under Lanfranc provided moral legitimacy and loyal administrators.
• The Harrying of the North eliminated the biggest military threat.
• Winning Hastings itself was the prerequisite for everything else.
Best answers will argue that William's 'greatest achievement' was the system as a whole — feudalism, castles, Church reform, and the Domesday Book worked together to create an unbreakable structure of control.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the disputed succession after William I's death in 1087.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification + 1 for supporting detail):
• Feature 1: William divided his lands between his sons (1) — Robert received Normandy while William Rufus received England, creating rival power centres (1).
• Feature 2: Odo of Bayeux led a revolt against William Rufus in 1088 (1) — he sided with Robert, but the revolt failed and Odo was exiled to Normandy permanently (1).
• Accept: Norman lords had to choose sides; William Rufus promised good government to win English support.
